- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Google released Gemini 4 Neon, promising "frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows."The model is live today through the API at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, above Carbon and Argon's introductory rate of $2/$10 (doubling to $4/$20 on December 1) and twice the price of Hydrogen at $1.50/$7.50.
> Neon offers a context window of about one million tokens and can produce up to one million output tokens. It handles text, images, video, audio, and PDFs, with support for Computer Use, code execution, file search, and grounding via Google Search and Maps. Image and audio generation aren't supported.
> Full specs are in the documentation. Benchmarks should follow in the next few hours. If Carbon and Argon are Google's counterparts to OpenAI's Astra or Anthropic's Fable, Neon is likely its Claude Opus or Sol equivalent. It's also Google's fourth new Gemini 4 model in four weeks.

### Trump’s latest land grab is an AI hub in the Philippines
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/96d7ba132d63f2da
- Primary Source: The Verge AI (https://www.theverge.com/policy/1036749/trump-ai-chip-data-center-us-philippines-pax-silica)
- Executive Summary: President Donald Trump was greeted by no less than five beauty queens when he landed in the Philippines on Tuesday, according to local news outlet Rappler. As he stepped onto the tarmac, a child handed him small US and Philippine flags. A band played “YMCA,” a staple at Trump rallies, as more girls in traditional bell-sleeved blouses and young men in wide-brimmed hats danced to the song. Outside the airport, hundreds of protesters packed streets bearing signs — and at least one prop casket — sa
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Justine Calma: Trump’s latest land grab is an AI hub in the Philippines
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] President Donald Trump was greeted by no less than five beauty queens when he landed in the Philippines on Tuesday, according to local news outlet Rappler.
* [Key Metrics] The agency expects to rake in close to $1 billion USD (about 60 billion in PHP Peso) from lease income over the first 25 years.
* [Key Position & Outlook] Trump’s latest land grab is an AI hub in the Philippines.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> President Donald Trump was greeted by no less than five beauty queens when he landed in the Philippines on Tuesday, according to local news outlet Rappler. As he stepped onto the tarmac, a child handed him small US and Philippine flags. A band played “YMCA,” a staple at Trump rallies, as more girls in traditional bell-sleeved blouses and young men in wide-brimmed hats danced to the song.
> Outside the airport, hundreds of protesters packed streets bearing signs — and at least one prop casket — saying “Trump out.” Others say “Reject Pax Silica,” the name for the US-led international initiative to secure chips and critical minerals used in the hardware fueling the AI boom.
> "Peace and prosperity for whom?"
> “Pax” comes from the Latin word for “peace, stability, and long-term prosperity,” the Pax Silica website proudly says. Yet the unspoken question — peace and prosperity for whom? — explains the whiplash between the Philippine government’s warm welcome of Trump and the public fury raging outside.
> Trump says he wants to “win AI” — whatever that means. As such, the US needs data centers full of GPUs to do it. With Americans increasingly opposed to data centers and chip factories being built in their communities, the US is now recruiting less affluent nations to take up some of the slack. Lawmakers from both the US and the Philippines are promising a slice of the riches that advances in generative AI are supposed to create. And that’s supposed to be worth the land razed, homes destroyed, and natural resources lost in the name of technological progress. In the Philippines, that’s taking the shape of a proposed 1,620-hectare (4,000 acres) hub for chip factories, processing plants for critical minerals, and data centers.
> At least two dozen countries have signed on to the Pax Silica initiative, and Trump was expected to pressure more to join while in the Philippines for events related to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. With Pax Silica, the US aims to insulate itself from China’s dominance in manufacturing semiconductors and processing critical minerals needed to make those chips. Trump held a bilateral meeting with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. Wednesday before heading to Shenzhen to meet with China’s President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin.
> Philippine and US officials are expected to sign a framework agreement by the end of the year for the jointly developed Pax Silica Economic Security Zone. The details are still murky and shrouded in NDAs. The Philippines’ Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) overseeing the plan expects an economic boom from minerals processing and chip manufacturing, with perhaps a data center or two on site. Meanwhile, human rights advocates who oppose the project warn that it will displace Indigenous residents, cutting them off from water resources on which they rely.
> “How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood?”
> “We do not want to give up our community,” Petronila Capiz-Muñoz, chieftain of the Indigenous Aeta Hungey tribe, told Human Rights Watch. “How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood? This is where we source our water, this is where we plant.” Capiz-Muñoz said BCDA officials have told residents that they’ll need to relocate by December to make way for development. Small farmers are also afraid the semiconductor hub will push them off their lands, according to Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch.
> There are layers of land-grabbing to unpack here.
> The Aeta are among the first people to inhabit the Philippines, believed to have arrived around 30,000 years ago. And yet the Aeta Hungey tribe has been trying since 1994 to secure an official certificate recognizing its ancestral domain in one of the areas now facing industrial development. But since the tribe hasn’t been granted that certificate, the BCDA can still claim the AI hub will be built “outside titled ancestral domains.”
> The agency says the project will be on public land located at the former Clark Air Base built in the early 1900s when the Philippines was a US territory. The Philippine constitution now only allows its own citizens to own private land. But the BCDA can offer leases lasting as long as 99 years to foreign developers. The agency expects to rake in close to $1 billion USD (about 60 billion in PHP Peso) from lease income over the first 25 years.
> "There are layers of land-grabbing to unpack here"
> The BCDA was in talks with around 30 different companies interested in setting up shop in Clark’s proposed AI hub, then-BCDA President and CEO Joshua Bingcang told reporters in July. He couldn’t name names, he said, because of NDAs — creating the same kind of opacity that has turned Americans against data centers on their home turf.
> He did mention, however, that an American energy company was conducting a feasibility study into building a liquefied natural gas (LNG) line and plant to meet the hub’s enormous electricity demand. Bingcang called LNG a clean fuel, but that’s provably false. LNG is primarily methane, a smog-forming pollutant that is an even more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide.
> Bingcang said in September that the Philippine government wanted to invite Nvidia, TSMC, and Apple. While one or two data center developers had expressed interest, according to Bingcang, most of the companies interested were “high tech” manufacturing firms. He has also described chip manufacturing as a “clean” industry, echoing corporate spin that’s been around since the start of Silicon Valley.
> At the first chip fabs in California, workers — many of them Filipino immigrants — donned “bunny suits” to assemble sensitive chips in environmentally controlled “clean rooms.” Little did they know that the gear they wore offered little protection against the harsh chemicals used in manufacturing, which also leaked out of storage tanks to contaminate soil and groundwater. When studies came out in the ’90s documenting disproportionately high rates of miscarriages among workers, companies pledged to phase out some of the chemicals linked to reproductive health risks. Around the same time, chip manufacturing started to move out of the US to Asia, where similar health problems stemming from the same chemicals cropped up even decades later.
> Chipmakers say their fabs have gotten much safer over the years, in part because more work is automated. Even so, the BCDA estimates that the AI hub will create up to 190,000 direct jobs. The BCDA, White House, and Philippine’s Malacañang Palace did not immediately respond to questions from The Verge.
> “I don’t want to date myself, but I knew your parents very well. They were great,” Trump told President Marcos during his visit. Marcos’ parents are estimated to have stolen up to $30 billion from government coffers over decades of rule before a people power movement ousted the current president’s father from the same office in the 1980s. But public memory, it seems, can be short.
> And skyrocketing demand for more powerful chips used for generative AI has raised fears among environmental and labor groups that history might repeat itself. Companies move fast and break things, leaving a toxic mess in their wake. And when Americans decide they’ve had enough in their own back yards, the industry sets up shop somewhere else where they think their customers aren’t paying attention and politicians are happy to look the other direction.

### Nvidia’s rise, visualized
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/97423cdd20723b1d
- Primary Source: The Verge AI (https://www.theverge.com/tech/1035924/nvidia-visualized-revenue-profit-earnings-after-huang)
- Executive Summary: If someone handed you $8,300 every second, what would you do? That’s how much pure profit Nvidia now makes. By the time you finish reading this paragraph, Nvidia will likely have cleared $45,000 and change. It’s easy to look at Nvidia, a company that just lost its visionary founder CEO due to a series of scandals, and think that the company and maybe the entire AI industry are in terrible trouble. Perhaps so? But I want you to understand: Nvidia isn’t your average semi-successful company that
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Sean Hollister: Nvidia’s rise, visualized
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] It’s easy to look at Nvidia, a company that just lost its visionary founder CEO due to a series of scandals, and think that the company and maybe the entire AI industry are in terrible trouble.
* [Key Metrics] If someone handed you $8,300 every second, what would you do.
* [Key Position & Outlook] Nvidia’s rise, visualized.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> If someone handed you $8,300 every second, what would you do? That’s how much pure profit Nvidia now makes. By the time you finish reading this paragraph, Nvidia will likely have cleared $45,000 and change.
> It’s easy to look at Nvidia, a company that just lost its visionary founder CEO due to a series of scandals, and think that the company and maybe the entire AI industry are in terrible trouble. Perhaps so?
> But I want you to understand: Nvidia isn’t your average semi-successful company that might tempt a new CEO to fix things that are broken. It is a company so staggeringly, mind-bogglingly successful it’ll do everything in its power not to rock the boat. There is so much money at stake.
> It’s so much money that when I heard about Jensen Huang’s resignation, my first thought was: I need a way to visualize this jaw-dropping amount of money for you. I want to show you that Nvidia has risen so far, so fast, that rival chipmakers AMD, Intel, and Qualcomm barely qualify as competition now.
> If you’re on a desktop OS, you could mouse over each dot in our chart above to see the staggering sums. But we built another way to visualize the rise of Nvidia I like even better. It’s a horizontal bar graph that not only puts Nvidia’s revenue growth in perspective, but shows you its monster profits right alongside them — plus the world events that made Nvidia a star.
> TL;DR: The crypto boom and the great GPU shortage have nothing on the AI boom. Those earlier periods saw Nvidia’s profits briefly peak at $1.24 billion and $3 billion a quarter respectively, while the rise of data centers has driven them to $65 billion per quarter with no sign of stopping.
> Yes, Jensen may have set a trillion dollars of Nvidia’s market cap on fire — from around $5 trillion at the start of November to “only” $3.6 trillion now — but the smoldering company is raking in $700 million in profit a day on average.
> Put another way: Nvidia could give a $1 million bonus to every one of its 42,000 employees, every three months, without running out of cash. Or, you know, Nvidia could end world hunger or provide clean water for everyone, now that it’s making over $200 billion in pure profit a year.
> Maybe that’d make people feel differently about data centers?
> But even if we stick to self-serving capitalism, you’re probably still a happy investor if you bought Nvidia a decade ago. A $1,000 investment 10 years ago is now worth over $67,000. You’d have over $1 million if you invested $15,000 back then.
> And make no mistake, Nvidia is sticking to capitalism. Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress just promised to return as much money to investors as possible on the company’s November 17th earnings call. “Going forward, we intend to return all excess free cash flow net of strategic uses to shareholders,” she announced. “All” is a lot more than the 50 percent baseline that Jensen promised five months ago.
> Nvidia isn’t the only company whose fortunes have risen this dramatically. RAMageddon revealed that just three companies — Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron — controlled nearly 90 percent of the entire global DRAM market, and those three have repeatedly signaled that they’d prefer to celebrate record profits instead of ramping up production too fast.
> But while their revenues and profits have been skyrocketing even faster over the past year or so, even Big RAM hasn’t caught the AI wave quite the same way as Nvidia. Samsung, of course, doesn’t just make memory — its revenue numbers include phones, tablets, TVs, home appliances, chips, displays, camera sensors, audio, networking equipment, medical equipment, and more.
> In the most recent quarter, Micron made $37.7 billion in profit, SK Hynix made $29.8 billion, and Samsung came in at around $55.3 billion, but they’re all shy of Nvidia’s $65.3 billion. Historically, RAM has also been a bit more cyclical: Both Micron and SK Hynix actually lost money in 2023 because they produced too much memory.
> On its latest earnings call, the first since cofounder Jensen Huang’s resignation, interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress reinforced the idea that Nvidia expects the good times to keep on rolling.
> Asked how things might change under new management, she suggested that they wouldn’t: “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual,” she said. She added that the company has secured the backing of customers and suppliers including TSMC, the all-important firm that actually fabricates Nvidia’s chips.
> “Our momentum is real, our demand is accelerating, our supply is growing. Our customers and partners are with us, and employees are committed,” she claimed. “We’ve got this.”
> Nvidia claims it’ll rake in even more money next quarter, with projected revenue of $130 billion. Profit may be proportionally smaller since gross margins are estimated to drop to 71–72 percent (compared to nearly 75 percent), but Kress said Nvidia intends to get them up as high as 73 percent next year.
> In other words: This astounding gravy train isn’t going anywhere. At least that’s the plan.
> Stevie Bonifield contributed to this story.

### Tech lawsuits defined 2026 — and lawmakers want more
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/78835c426e98c9a4
- Primary Source: The Verge AI (https://www.theverge.com/policy/1036935/congress-forced-arbitration-deepfakes-defiance-act)
- Executive Summary: With just a few weeks remaining, lawmakers are trying to pass new protections for victims of online harm before the end of 2026, targeting deepfake creators and online platforms that block users from filing lawsuits. On Tuesday, members of a Senate Judiciary subcommittee hosted a hearing calling for the end of forced arbitration for online harms. Their immediate target was Roblox, which they accused of evading legal complaints about children allegedly groomed on the platform by enforcing its ow
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Lauren Feiner: Tech lawsuits defined 2026 — and lawmakers want more
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] Their immediate target was Roblox, which they accused of evading legal complaints about children allegedly groomed on the platform by enforcing its ow.
* [Regulatory & Investigation Focus] Tech lawsuits defined 2026 — and lawmakers want more.
* [Key Position & Outlook] Tech lawsuits defined 2026 — and lawmakers want more.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> With just a few weeks remaining, lawmakers are trying to pass new protections for victims of online harm before the end of 2026, targeting deepfake creators and online platforms that block users from filing lawsuits.
> On Tuesday, members of a Senate Judiciary subcommittee hosted a hearing calling for the end of forced arbitration for online harms. Their immediate target was Roblox, which they accused of evading legal complaints about children allegedly groomed on the platform by enforcing its own forced arbitration clause against users who agreed to the terms as minors, in some cases even under the age of 10. Separately, a few blocks away, Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) and Laurel Lee (R-FL) brought hotel heiress Paris Hilton to Capitol Hill to advocate for the Defiance Act, which would let victims of nonconsensual intimate deepfakes sue their creators.
> “The best thing we can do in terms of enforcement is we can open up the courthouse doors,” Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO), who chairs the Judiciary subcommittee, told reporters after the Roblox hearing. “The more I see these companies evade regulations, the more I think there is nothing as powerful as a jury.” Hawley introduced a new bill with ranking member Dick Durbin (D-IL) to render arbitration agreements unenforceable for disputes over alleged child sexual exploitation or “child cyber injury,” which could include “reputational harm, mental suffering,” or death.
> “The best thing we can do in terms of enforcement is we can open up the courthouse doors”
> Roblox has sought to enforce its arbitration clause in lawsuits it’s facing over allegations that users were groomed on the gaming platform as minors, despite the company’s claims of protections. Roblox is facing about 180 lawsuits in a consolidated case over its alleged role in failing to protect children. Under the arbitration process, the public would not get to see legal discovery like the kind that’s come to light under recent cases against Meta. Hawley called the jury system “corruption-proof” and “an incredibly big hammer.”
> Roblox has denied that it’s trying to dodge accountability. “Safety has been central to Roblox since we launched. We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” Roblox’s global head of public policy Nicky Jackson Colaço said in a statement. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”
> Congress has only a little more than three more weeks left in session before the end of the year, and a new Democratic majority will be sworn in come January. Republicans are expected to do their best to push through President Donald Trump’s nominees for judgeships and executive branch posts like FCC commissioner in the lame-duck session, as well as try to pass year-end bills like the National Defense Authorization Act, which often includes a range of other policy items. But some lawmakers are holding out hope that they can open up courthouses to new litigation over deepfake abuse and child predation.
> Litigation has become one of the more successful ways for survivors of online harm to seek change. Congress has failed to pass many prominent child safety, privacy, and consumer protection bills, though it has begun to tackle the deepfake issue through the Take It Down Act. At the same time, attorneys general and individual plaintiffs have collected significant settlements and legal wins despite the broad scope of tech’s legal shield, Section 230. If bills like the Defiance Act or those seeking to end forced arbitration were to pass, tech companies and perpetrators of online harms could become vulnerable to a new wave of legal challenges.
> “You will be amazed by how quickly the company will change its behavior once it is sued in public court”
> In addition to Hawley and Durbin’s bill about forced arbitration, Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Katie Britt (R-AL), and Cory Booker (D-NJ) introduced a similar bill with a slightly different approach, including explicitly covering data privacy violations. At the Roblox hearing, Northwestern University law professor Myriam Gilles, an expert on forced arbitration, said she’s testified before Congress many times on this topic, but “never expected to come before this body to talk about its use against 9 year olds.” Passing either proposal, she said, would have a profound impact. “You will be amazed by how quickly the company will change its behavior once it is sued in public court.”
> The Defiance Act would let victims of nonconsensual intimate deepfakes sue their creators for damages, in an attempt to raise the cost of creating these kinds of images. Hilton visited Washington earlier this year to share how an intimate non-deepfake video of her at age 19 shared without her consent impacted her life, and she used her story to advocate for the Defiance Act. At Tuesday’s press conference, she said she would come back to Congress as many times as necessary for the bill to become law. “Some people might have thought that was the end of my fight,” Hilton said. “But when I make a promise to survivors, I keep it.”
> Hilton said over 50 million people have been victimized by sexually explicit deepfakes. “For me personally, strangers have created over 100,000 AI-generated explicit images and videos portraying me in the most graphic and disturbing ways imaginable,” Hilton said. “If this can happen to someone with my resources and my platform, imagine how powerless a young girl might feel facing this completely alone.”
> Hilton’s comments were followed by Elliston Berry, an advocate who said a classmate made an explicit deepfake image of her friend group “from an innocent social media post” when she was 14, and distributed it throughout her school. “In a matter of seconds, my sense of security disappeared,” she said. “For me, the Defiance Act means recognition that victims deserve to be heard, that their experience matters, and that their right to seek justice should not depend on how quickly technology advances.”

### Microsoft is replacing outside AI models in its own products with cheaper in-house alternatives
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/19a14ae4e81ee699
- Primary Source: THE DECODER (https://the-decoder.com/microsoft-is-replacing-outside-ai-models-in-its-own-products-with-cheaper-in-house-alternatives/)
- Executive Summary: Microsoft AI unveiled seven in-house models at Ignite to replace third-party models across its product suite, including GitHub Copilot and Microsoft 365. The primary driver is to mitigate surging costs from continuous AI agent tasks, with Microsoft claiming superior price-to-performance ratios compared to existing OpenAI and Anthropic offerings.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Microsoft AI (MAI) (Microsoft Ignite conference): Launched seven in-house models to replace third-party alternatives
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] Reduce high token spending and operational costs for enterprise agents
* [Key Metrics] In GitHub Copilot, MAI Code 2 costs $0.
* [Industry Impact & Outlook] Microsoft reshapes AI business model through ecosystem integration.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Microsoft AI (MAI) is targeting always-on AI agents with new models for code, security, images, speech, and routing. The main yardstick is the lineup of its own partner, OpenAI.
> At its Ignite conference, MAI unveiled seven new models, releasing them in a single batch rather than spread across the year, just as it did at Build in June. Microsoft is positioning the new lineup primarily on price-to-performance. The company cites rapidly rising token spending among customers that want to run AI agents around the clock. Its code models target everyday enterprise coding tasks and aren't yet optimized for harder work such as foundational research or long-horizon agentic workflows, Microsoft says.
> ### MAI Code 2 approaches GPT-6.1 Sol and Opus 5.5 at a promotional price
> According to Microsoft, MAI Code 2 averages 98 percent of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance across four benchmarks at 40 percent of the cost. Against Claude Opus 5.5, it reaches 96 percent of the performance at 5 percent of the cost. Microsoft tested on DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas, and FrontierCode v1.1. Three of the tests ran on Microsoft's internal MSBench platform using the GitHub Copilot CLI without sub-agents. Microsoft is calculating a 50 percent promotional discount for its own model.
> In blind comparisons of frontend work such as UIs, games, data visualizations, and SVG graphics, human evaluators preferred MAI Code 2's output 64 percent of the time over GPT-6 Sol, Microsoft says.
> The successor to MAI-Code-1.1-Flash, MAI Code 2 Flash, is designed for code explanations, targeted edits, and routine fixes. It's said to match GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 65 and 20 percent of their respective costs.
> Microsoft derived MAI Work Flash from the Flash model. It runs in Microsoft 365 and Fabric IQ. On internal Excel and PowerPoint benchmarks, it matches GPT-6 Luna, Microsoft says. In Word, it performs similarly to GPT-6.1 Sol while consuming about 42 percent fewer input tokens. For generating DAX queries in Power BI, it outperforms GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Opus 5.5.
> In GitHub Copilot, MAI Code 2 costs $0.50 per million input tokens and $2.50 per million output tokens at the promotional price through May 17, 2027, then $1 and $5. MAI Code 2 Flash costs $0.05 and $0.25 until then, rising to $0.10 and $0.50.
> ### Security model with a cleaned-up benchmark
> MAI Cyber 2 Flash solves 92.3 percent of the tasks in the CyberGym-E2E vulnerability benchmark, Microsoft says. GPT-6 Astra reaches 91.5 percent but needs twice the reasoning budget. Per task, the MAI model costs less than 2 percent of GPT-6 Astra, with per-token costs at one hundredth. On WebExploitBench, it scores 40.4 percent, ahead of GPT-5.6 Cyber at 38.4 percent.
> During evaluation, Microsoft found that 10 percent of the roughly 900 CyberGym tasks draw on the same open-source projects and vulnerability reports as parts of its own training data. The reference solutions never entered training, the company says. Microsoft removed those tasks for all models anyway and scored only the rest.
> A comparison with GPT-6 Cyber is missing so far. The model is available only to selected customers. Agentic benchmarks with tools still need extra safety measures, Microsoft says. The company plans to publish those results in the coming weeks.
> The context window spans one million tokens, four times the size of MAI Cyber 1.1 Flash. Output tokens cost 86 percent less than the predecessor's. MAI Cyber models already handle nearly 40 percent of scans on Microsoft's security platform MDASH, the press release states.
> Microsoft lists MAI Cyber 2 Flash at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, compared with $10 and $50 for GPT-6 Astra. On CyberGym-E2E, that works out to $0.45 per task instead of $34.38.
> ### Microsoft's decision model now runs on Google's Gemma
> Microsoft-Decision-1.1 handles routing, classification, prioritization, and workflow control. The model picks from developer-approved actions and returns calibrated confidence scores. When uncertainty is high, apps can escalate instead of acting on a wrong decision. If information is incomplete, the model is designed to abstain.
> Its foundation is Google's mixture-of-experts model Gemma 4 26B A4B. The predecessor was built on Qwen3.5-9B. Microsoft trained the new model with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on hundreds of synthetic and licensed datasets and runs it on a proprietary inference engine.
> On the Decision Index v2.1 from Artificial Analysis, Decision 1.1 scores 68 points. That's six more than its predecessor and above Jev 1.14, Gemini Decision 1, and GPT-6 Luna (Decisions). Microsoft also tested it on 102 internal benchmarks with more than 385,000 questions, where it achieves the highest average accuracy among eight decision models.
> The model now accepts images, including screenshots. In Copilot, it decides whether a request goes to Copilot or Cowork. It performs as accurately as a large language model but 2.2 times faster and 4.4 times cheaper, Microsoft says. In Cowork, its Auto function controls how much reasoning effort a task receives.
> Microsoft charges $0.042 per million input tokens, or $0.05 in the EU data zone. Output tokens are free.
> Another specialized model appears in the Book of News for Ignite. Microsoft-Retriever-1 gathers relevant information from enterprise documents for agents in Foundry IQ. Instead of running a single search, the model plans its queries, evaluates the results, and issues follow-ups until it has enough material for a well-grounded answer. Microsoft says that's faster and more efficient than previous methods. Retriever-1 launches as a preview. The Model Router in Foundry now also selects automatically from an expanded pool of models.
> ### Image editing just ahead of OpenAI
> MAI Image 2.7 leads the Artificial Analysis image-editing leaderboard with 1,215 Elo points from 5,478 votes. It's four points ahead of GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst (max) at one-fifth the cost. For text-to-image generation, the model ranks fourth on that leaderboard. MAI Image 2.7 costs about $35 per 1,000 images. Flash costs about $10.
> The model can change the color, material, or position of individual objects without altering the rest of the image. It also generates transparent backgrounds. The smaller Flash variant costs less than a third and powers Canvas, a new image editor in MAI Labs. MAI Image has been the default model in Bing Image Creator since June. Adobe, Figma Weave, Minute (Sports Illustrated), Wirestock, and Manus work with MAI Image, Microsoft says.
> ### Speech model compatible with OpenAI's API
> MAI Realtime 1 is Microsoft's first speech-to-speech model. It's designed to handle interruptions, wait until speakers finish, and recognize requests even with background noise. For harder tasks, it falls back to a more powerful reasoning engine billed per token. The base rate is charged per audio minute. On Big Bench Audio, τ-Voice, and tests with Dynamics 365, it outperforms GPT Realtime 2.1, Microsoft says.
> Because it's compatible with the OpenAI Realtime API, existing voice apps can switch over easily. Agoda and Reservations.ai are testing the model. Microsoft also plans to bring it to the Dynamics 365 Contact Center and Dragon Copilot, where nurses would use it to practice patient conversations.
> Dragon Copilot Transcribe, based on MAI Transcribe 2, now handles all doctor-patient transcriptions in Dragon Copilot. That amounts to 10 million conversations per month, Microsoft says. In multilingual workflows, the error rate drops by half. For its own large models, Microsoft now uses the Maia 200 chip, the second generation of its AI accelerator, said to deliver 1.7 times more tokens per watt.
> Microsoft charges one US cent per audio minute. Reasoning costs an extra $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens.
> ### Licensed weights available only through the Microsoft account team
> With MAI Licensed Weights, companies can fine-tune MAI models with their own data and run them in their own Azure environment. Data and customizations stay with the customer. Microsoft says it will use them for training its own models only with explicit consent.
> The company positions the offering as an alternative to open weights, whose provenance and behavior are hard for enterprises to verify. One example is US carrier AT&T, where a customized model for 5G network operations analysis reportedly outperformed GPT-6.1 Sol on standard tasks at roughly one-fiftieth of the cost. A launch date and pricing are still pending. Interested companies should contact their Microsoft account team. The offering is set to arrive "shortly"through Microsoft's Frontier Company program.
> MAI Code 2 and Code 2 Flash are available in GitHub Copilot, with Code 2 Flash also in a limited preview in Foundry. OpenRouter, Vercel, Hermes, Open Code, and Kilo are expected to follow. MAI Image 2.7 and Flash are in public preview in Foundry and on fal, Genspark, OpenRouter, and Vercel. Decision 1.1 is generally available in Foundry, on OpenRouter, and through Vercel's AI Gateway. MAI Realtime 1 can be tried in MAI Labs and is available as a Foundry preview, free until the public preview launches. MAI Cyber 2 Flash is exclusive to Microsoft's security products. In MDASH, it will automatically replace the existing model in the MAI profile for eligible customers starting mid-December.
> In April, Microsoft and OpenAI restructured their partnership. OpenAI can now sell its products through any cloud provider, but Azure remains the primary cloud partner. Microsoft holds a non-exclusive license to OpenAI's models and products through 2032.

### What is Nvidia without AI’s sugar daddy in charge?
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/cb3094d728a94851
- Primary Source: The Verge AI (https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/1036776/nvidia-earnings-kress-jensen-huang-petition)
- Executive Summary: Following Jensen Huang's departure due to personal misconduct, interim CEO Colette Kress held her first all-hands meeting at Nvidia. To counter market concerns regarding supply chain stability without Huang, Kress confirmed supply agreements remain valid through the end of the decade and announced accelerated salary and equity packages to address internal unrest.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Interim CEO Colette Kress, Board Chair Harvey C. Jones (Nvidia all-hands meeting): Announced accelerated pay raises and equity, reaffirmed supply chain agreements
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] Managing leadership crisis and potential brain drain following Huang's exit
* [Key Fact Detail] Following Jensen Huang's departure due to personal misconduct, interim CEO Colette Kress held her first all-hands meeting at Nvidia.
* [Industry Impact & Outlook] Kress's focus on fiscal discipline may signal the end of the company's historically aggressive customer-financing strategy, shifting Nvidia's supply chain dominance to rely more on legal contract enforcement rather than personal endorsements.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> If the glorious AI revolution rests entirely on the well-being of one man, AI is perhaps not as robust a technology as I had previously been led to believe. Nonetheless, chunks of Silicon Valley are now insisting he is indispensable. For instance, if Elon Musk is telling the truth, then Jensen Huang (the former CEO of Nvidia, a company with a market cap of about $3 trillion) has been making deals that were “a handshake with Jensen” with suppliers — “not a written contract,” Musk wrote.
> Fascinating stuff to tell shareholders. But after listening to Nvidia’s first earnings call with its new CEO, Colette Kress, I do think something may have shifted. In her former role as CFO, Kress generally told Huang to stop spending so much money on financing its customers, because telling the CEO to stop spending so much goddamn money is the CFO’s job. Apparently he belittled her about this, but that’s the CEO–CFO relationship, baby! Anyway she’s the boss now, at least temporarily. I think it’s reasonable to assume that though Nvidia has for years been the AI industry’s sugar daddy, without Huang and his handshakes in the picture, it may be less liberal with its cash.
> "Kress shot down the idea that Huang’s departure would lead to a brain drain within Nvidia"
> Kress’ job was never going to be easy. Even without tantrums from the likes of Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Musk, both of whom seem to have a lot of free time for guys who are ostensibly running multibillion-dollar companies, having to steer a company after an event on the scale of Huang’s meltdown is a miserable task. But this woman also is now having to deal with a bunch of guys publicly insisting that Huang was the only reason Nvidia succeeded. It amused me on the call that she did the thing I often do when men decide they can bully me, which is to tap in another man who is theoretically or actually in charge of me — and so on the call, Nvidia board Chair Harvey C. Jones politely told these losers to get bent. The board does not intend to reinstate Huang, and the company won’t be taking questions about him.
> On the call, Kress pointedly noted that Nvidia’s agreements with suppliers last through the end of the decade, so I suppose we must entertain the possibility that when it comes to the handshake deals, Musk is, once again, lying. This is an important thing, though — as SemiAnalysis noted in its bizarrely conspiratorial post on the situation, Nvidia is successful because it has choked off the supply chain.
> Kress also shot down the idea that Huang’s departure would lead to a brain drain within Nvidia, or the kind of open internal revolt that got Sam Altman reinstated at OpenAI during “the blip” in 2023. She told investors that “our employees, we believe, are committed. They are committed to doing their life’s work at Nvidia.” Nvidia’s employees have “been working seamlessly on what they need to complete,” she added. “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual.” I’m sure we’ll hear more about this in the coming days, but unlike with Altman, Huang resigned, and we all know why. And while some employees support reinstating Huang, I notice that there’s a real dearth of “we’ll quit with him” in those sentiments.
> I don’t think this is going to shut the Branch Nvidians up, but I do think the board doesn’t have another choice here. Hilariously, we learned this weekend that Nvidia did not buy complete directors’ and officers’ insurance. While the individual executives’ and board members’ personal assets are shielded from lawsuits that stem from its executives’ behavior, the company is not. So if someone, or perhaps several someones, were to file a suit because of, say, Huang’s personal life and its damaging effects on the stock price, Nvidia itself is on the hook.
> "The scandal isn’t mainly about the affairs, as much fun as we all have been having with them"
> This is to say nothing of the Securities and Exchange Commission’s investigation — which, given how cliqued up Huang was with President Donald Trump, may be investigating on his behalf rather than investigating him — or the California attorney general going on Bloomberg TV to say that he was going to start kicking the tires on an investigation, or Huang and general counsel Tim Teter’s upcoming congressional testimony. The three actual lawyers left at the Department of Justice may be doing their own investigation, too. Elizabeth Warren seems mad. Marco Rubio’s name has been publicly attached in stories on the leaks, which makes me a little suspicious about who’s been doing the leaking.
> A reminder: The scandal isn’t mainly about the affairs, as much fun as we all have been having with them. It is about Nvidia customers allegedly circumventing a ban on selling chips to China. The scandal is already big enough that US policy has been altered; the Department of Commerce informed us all on November 16th that there were new restrictions on selling chips to countries such as Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. Also, data centers around the world need licenses from the US to lease compute to companies headquartered in China.
> “No one could tell them ‘no’ or put them in their place.”
> You may be wondering how these restrictions will affect Nvidia’s sales. The company also addressed this, though somewhat obliquely: It raised its forecast, saying that revenue will grow by 75 percent next year. Still, given that Singapore alone was responsible for $104 billion of revenue in 2025, I am curious about the number; at the time, it was the second-biggest geographic area by revenue, dwarfed only by the US. I can’t tell you how much Singaporean sales matter to Nvidia now, because around the time that Singaporean sales reportedly started to represent half the company’s revenue, Nvidia switched its reporting methodology. The company had previously noted that “most shipments associated with Singapore revenue were to locations other than Singapore and shipments to Singapore were insignificant.” Notably, Megaspeed had a Singapore address — and was the subject of a truncated Commerce Department investigation into whether its chips were being diverted to China. Fun stuff!
> You know what else is fun? Jensen Huang’s children are still at the company, at least as far as anyone knows. His daughter Madison, described as Huang’s “chief of staff” by The New York Times, even helped direct Nvidia’s response to inquiries about Megaspeed, which have been mounting now for a year, the Financial Times reported. Her husband, Nico Caprez, “was promoted to a role that covered international deals with cloud computing clients in Asia” around the time those inquiries were getting started. “They had a lot of power and influence and were allowed to operate unchecked,” an anonymous source told the FT. “No one could tell them ‘no’ or put them in their place.”
> His kids — one of them, Spencer, ran a bar before his role at Nvidia — likely haven’t endeared themselves to their colleagues, based on some of the reporting now trickling out about them. What was Spencer doing at Nvidia? Unknown. “Some executives said they had never encountered Spencer Huang in the course of business,” The Wall Street Journal wrote.
> "As a person who loves mess, I think the Branch Nvidians should keep this shit coming"
> Employing the CEO’s relatives was already a governance risk. If the outside agitation continues to reinstate Jensen Huang, there are three key lambs that Nvidia can slaughter, and all of them are his relatives. I suppose the thing I find most astonishing is that Huang doesn’t see the writing on the wall; he has posted that if “the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” The post was met with, among other things, Altman posting a green heart in response.
> Now, as a person who loves mess, I think the Branch Nvidians should keep this shit coming. I mean, Huang can nominate two people to the board of directors before the company’s shareholder meeting next year. Let’s have a stupid proxy fight and see what else leaks about Huang’s leadership and children! Of course, that will be difficult for Kress to manage — but that’s I guess what she’s getting paid for.
> Up until now, Kress had been trying to rein in Huang’s spending on the AI ecosystem — financing, investments, and so on — in a huge swath of companies, according to stories in The Information and The Wall Street Journal. According to the Journal’s story, Huang noted that the vaunted deals he’d made with suppliers “were coming at him like an ‘avalanche,’” while “major cloud providers were running away from Nvidia.” This does explain Nvidia’s role as the sugar daddy for the neocloud industry. Kress reportedly pushed back on some of its agreements, apparently significantly downsizing a financial commitment to OpenAI among other things. Now, while she’ll be spending plenty of her time managing the fallout from Huang’s departure, she won’t be directly fighting with him over Nvidia’s finances.
> "It publicly tells us there are limitations on what Nvidia is willing to support"
> On the earnings call, analyst Stacy Rasgon of Bernstein Research asked about a new paragraph he’d noticed in the earnings release about neoclouds. Nvidia had been supplying guarantees to some neoclouds by saying it would purchase compute if no one else would. The new paragraph reads, in part, “Our commitments take effect only if the neoclouds secure financing to purchase the data center infrastructure products and the related compute capacity is deployed, made operational, and accepted by us.” Kress clarified that this meant that if neoclouds’ buildout was delayed — or they otherwise had a challenge in building the warehouse to stick the chips in — Nvidia’s guarantee “doesn’t exist anymore,” she said. “Is it new? No. Did we change anything? No,” she said.
> I have no way of knowing if this language had been ready to go in the press release before Huang resigned, but it does seem notable all the same. It publicly tells us there are limitations on what Nvidia is willing to support. And knowing Kress wanted Huang to spend less on this stuff, I think it tees us up for an interesting period. Passing under the radar last week were some indications that the Federal Reserve may be about to do an interest rate hike, which is trouble for a number of companies, such as CoreWeave, that rely on debt for their data center buildouts. If we are entering a period where financing is more expensive or more difficult to get, we may see some neoclouds falter. The new paragraph in the earnings release suggests that Nvidia wants us all to know that it’s not going to bail them out forever. Bring Huang back if you want, I guess, but even he can’t control the Fed — or the increasingly odd outlook for data center financing. In the coming months, Nvidia may be better off with a woman who wants to keep the costs down.
> You know who is getting money under Kress, though? Nvidia staff. They can expect raises and equity in December.

### OpenAI says its models delivered a year's worth of chip optimization on top of AMD's own engineering
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/15425cccd9ae521e
- Primary Source: THE DECODER (https://the-decoder.com/openai-says-its-models-delivered-a-years-worth-of-chip-optimization-on-top-of-amds-own-engineering/)
- Executive Summary: OpenAI collaborated with AMD to achieve a 14% PPA improvement on AMD's flagship GPU within five months using AI-assisted design. Additionally, OpenAI has tested its first custom inference chip, 'Jalapeño', and is working with Synopsys on an AI-driven chip design model to streamline hardware iteration.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] OpenAI, AMD, Synopsys (AI hardware engineering): Achieved 14% PPA gain, developed custom 'Jalapeño' chip
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] Overcoming compute bottlenecks and hardware supply chain reliance
* [Key Metrics] OpenAI collaborated with AMD to achieve a 14% PPA improvement on AMD's flagship GPU within five months using AI-assisted design.
* [Key Position & Outlook] By deepening ties with silicon vendors and entering the EDA process, OpenAI is effectively formalizing its training-optimization expertise to gain design-level control over high-performance computing hardware.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Working with AMD, OpenAI achieved up to 14 percent PPA improvement (power, performance, and chip area) on AMD's flagship GPU IP in less than five months. According to OpenAI, that equals about a year's worth of progress on top of designs AMD's engineers had already optimized for years. AMD has already folded some of the changes into a design sent to manufacturing, OpenAI says.
> The same method also helped with Jalapeño, OpenAI's first custom inference chip. In tests with open RISC-V processor cores, the new GPT-6.2 Astra model delivered the best results across model generations. OpenAI is also working with Synopsys on GPT-Synopsys, a model that uses Synopsys's EDA tools to make AI-assisted chip design more broadly accessible.
> Anthropic is using AI in chip work too. Its Mythos model handled prompt processing for a model on AMD MI355X GPUs in just three days instead of the six to twelve months Anthropic says the task normally takes. The company now runs Claude on four chip families to optimize cost and performance per dollar.

### Disney’s new Star Wars animatronics interact with guests using AI
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/8251fd94967d214f
- Primary Source: The Verge AI (https://www.theverge.com/tech/1036729/disney-star-wars-anzellans-animatronic-amazon-aws-cloud-ai)
- Executive Summary: Walt Disney Imagineering R&D has unveiled three new Audio-Animatronic prototypes that utilize AWS cloud AI to provide real-time responses to guest interactions. While AI manages the interaction logic, all movements and dialogue remain within pre-scripted boundaries to ensure thematic consistency for Disney park characters.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Walt Disney Imagineering R&D (AWS re:Invent / Disney Parks): Developed AI-powered interactive animatronics
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] Enhance immersive experiences in theme parks
* [Key Fact Detail] Walt Disney Imagineering R&D has unveiled three new Audio-Animatronic prototypes that utilize AWS cloud AI to provide real-time responses to guest interactions.
* [Key Position & Outlook] By keeping the models cloud-based and strictly bound to pre-scripted logic, Disney demonstrates a priority for controllability and safety when deploying generative AI in commercial entertainment.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> As advanced and lifelike as the animatronic characters at Disney parks have become, they typically either stick to predefined movements and routines, or there’s an out of sight puppeteer helping make their behavior appear more spontaneous. That could soon change as Walt Disney Imagineering R&D has revealed three new Audio-Animatronic prototypes that rely on Amazon’s AWS cloud and AI capabilities to respond in unique ways to guest interactions in real-time.
> The three animatronics, named Vilo Vele, Kado Bre’a, and Jibu Bre’a, are based on the Star Wars alien characters called the Anzellans that were featured in The Mandalorian and Grogu film released earlier this year. The tiny bots will make their first public appearance in Las Vegas later this month where attendees of the AWS re:Invent conference will have a chance to interact with them, although the characters, and the technology powering them, could eventually find its way into Star Wars: Galaxy’s Edge and other attractions at Disney’s parks.
> Unlike Disney’s Olaf robot that recently debuted, there’s no one secretly using a Steam Deck gaming handheld to bring the Anzellans to life. The animatronics instead each have hidden cameras and microphones they use to capture guest movements and verbal interactions which are processed by multiple AI models running on AWS cloud servers. One “fast-decision model” generates quick responses such as the animatronics quickly making eye contact so it appears as if they’re paying attention, while larger models plan out longer interactions.
> However, the Anzellans movements and verbal responses aren’t generated on the fly by AI. Every movement and line of dialogue that’s selected and triggered by the models is prewritten by Disney Imagineers to ensure the animations stay true to each character, including unique personality quirks for each one. Although AI helps guide their actions, the Anzellans never deviate from the script.

### Inside Nvidia’s First Post-Jensen All-Hands: Pay Raises and More Equity
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/27416b3b3654f84e
- Primary Source: Wired AI (https://www.wired.com/story/inside-nvidias-first-all-hands-without-jensen-huang-as-ceo/)
- Executive Summary: Security researchers have identified a surge in cyberattacks against global banks and governments using Artex, an open-source AI penetration framework. The tool integrates reconnaissance, exploitation, and data exfiltration into a 'point-and-shoot' workflow, significantly lowering technical barriers and compressing attack timelines from days to hours.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Cybercriminal syndicates (Global cyberspace): Executing automated penetration attacks via Artex
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] Increased efficiency and lower barrier to entry
* [Regulatory & Investigation Focus] Security researchers have identified a surge in cyberattacks against global banks and governments using Artex, an open-source AI penetration framework.
* [Official Stance & Demand] The emergence of tools like Artex confirms that LLM reasoning is being scaled across entire attack chains, rendering static defensive rules ineffective against dynamic, multi-objective intelligent threats.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress made her first address to the staff on Wednesday and just minutes into the meeting told employees that they can expect pay raises and more equity in December, months ahead of schedule, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED.
> “So I’m here to tell you, the best thing that we want to do is to take care of each and every single employee that is here and to make sure that you feel good about this company and you do not worry about your comp,” she said.
> Questions about compensation were the most common among the 700 submitted ahead of the meeting, Kress said. She said the next-most common request was for transparency from the board.
> Kress’ comments came during the first companywide meeting following the resignation of Jensen Huang as CEO last week. Huang had led the computer graphics chip maker since cofounding it 33 years ago, and his presentations during the quarterly town halls internally had become a much anticipated and memorable spectacle for some of the company’s nearly 49,000 employees. Information rarely leaked from the meetings in the past. Nvidia declined to comment for this story.
> But now Nvidia is facing an extraordinary leadership crisis. Huang resigned amid allegations of extramarital affairs, including potentially with a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia’s board chair Harvey Jones said on Tuesday that Huang disclosed “personal behavior” contrary to the company’s policies and norms and wouldn’t be invited back.
> During the companywide meeting on Wednesday, Jones reiterated that the board accepted Huang’s resignation due to his personal conduct and “lack of candor.” He said the company wouldn’t find a “Jensen clone,” but that there are “dynamic leaders out there, with demonstrated intellect, high-tech engineering experience, strategic thinking, cultural compatibility, and a track record of success.” He added, “We will not compromise our requirements for the sake of expediency” and that the board would accept employee suggestions on the CEO search.
> Thousands of employees have apparently lobbied for Huang’s reinstatement. Several well-known tech executives signed a public petition, with about 200,000 purported backers urging the same. Instead, the board is searching internally and externally for a replacement at one of the world’s most valuable companies and one of the biggest drivers of the generative AI boom.
> Huang’s departures and a slew of government investigations into him and Nvidia have rattled investors. But on Tuesday, Nvidia reported better-than-expected financial results and forecast growing sales in the years to come. Shares were up about 5 percent on Wednesday.
> One concern investors have expressed is whether Nvidia might see a brain drain of top talent. Many employees have stayed at Nvidia for Huang and his vision. Nvidia could also be perceived as a less desirable place for new and emerging talent to work, with its leadership in flux, during an especially critical time as competition in the AI chips market grows.
> On Tuesday’s third-quarter earnings call, an analyst from Bank of America Securities asked Kress directly about her “message” to Nvidia investors about talent retention, as well as the company’s overall durability and financial strategy through this major upheaval. Kress replied that “probably the most important thing” company leaders are thinking through right now is stabilizing its employee ranks.
> “We are always thinking about our employees. Like every community out there, there are diverse opinions,” Kress said. “We will take care of our employees during this transition to make sure they are safe and make sure the work can be done in the current environment.”
> In a brief question-and-answer session with Kress during the all-hands meeting Wednesday, Nvidia cofounder Chris Malachowsky addressed how the company could maintain its prized culture going forward.
> He recalled how he, Huang, and other cofounders thought it was “nonsense” to put cultural values up on posters. Instead, they want it instilled in “the way you behave, the way you work together, and the way you work,” and he believes that will stand the test of time. “We’re going to be fine,” he said.
> Kress ended the meeting, which lasted about 50 minutes, by comparing Nvidia’s employees to “90,000 people packed into the sweatiest, hottest” University of Florida football game.
> In the third quarter, “every single person sings,” she said. “It is impressive to see them all together, all in harmony singing that song … Do you know what? We’re gonna hear that song, guys. And I believe in all of you, that you will help sing it. Nvidia, we’ve got this.”
> Updated: 11/18/2026 1:26 p.m. EST: Updated with new details on comments made during the Nvidia all-hands meeting.

### Artex Is Criminals’ New Favorite ‘Point-and-Shoot’ AI Hacking Tool
- Canonical URL: https://ainewsradar.xyz/news/fad07a5ab0e510f7
- Primary Source: Wired AI (https://www.wired.com/story/artex-ai-hacking-tools/)
- Executive Summary: Independent evaluation firm Vals AI found that leading models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google lack effective safeguards against use in autonomous weapon systems. Experiments demonstrated that through 'video game' framing, models could be manipulated into marking civilians, medics, and surrendering soldiers as targets for drone strikes with minimal refusal.
- Key Verified Facts:
* [Core Event] Vals AI, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google (AI weaponization testing): Models found susceptible to assisting autonomous drone strikes
* [Root Cause & Mechanism] Safety filters fail under specific contextual prompting
* [Market & Financial Detail] Independent evaluation firm Vals AI found that leading models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google lack effective safeguards against use in autonomous weapon systems.
* [Key Position & Outlook] Once models are detached from reality via 'gamification' prompts, safety boundaries dissolve, posing a severe regulatory challenge for high-stakes AI applications.
- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> Over the past year, security researchers have warned that AI agents could vastly speed up cybercriminals’ ability to launch cyberattacks, breach companies, and ultimately steal money, data, or sensitive information from those compromised systems. For at least one subset of hackers, it appears that era has now arrived.
> Since around the end of August, multiple companies, government agencies, and banks around the world have been targeted by cybercriminals adopting a new wave of AI-powered penetration testing tools. These setups —many of which mimic legitimate defensive penetration testing techniques—use LLMs to autonomously scan potential hacking targets and attempt to force their way into poorly secured networks, then carry out attack plans written by human operators.
> Dozens of these AI penetration frameworks or “harnesses,” which detail how an AI model should carry out cybersecurity testing or attacks, are increasingly being linked to real-world attacks. The tools do not introduce new ways to attack websites or servers and are not sophisticated, according to alerts from around half a dozen security companies. Instead, they allow cybercriminals to launch attacks at speeds that would be impossible for humans to do.
> Hackers also don’t need to be skilled to use the tools, researchers say, and attacks that would have taken days are completed in just hours. “Agentic frameworks have progressed from experimental use to sustained, multi-objective offensive operations that run with minimal human intervention,” CJ Moses, AWS’s chief information security officer, wrote in a company blog post recently.
> The most prominent of these tools is Artex. Written in the programming language Go, the open-source framework was first published on GitHub in July by a pseudonymous developer using the handle Autumn-27, and it’s been spreading across some hacker communities ever since. Artex has been used across all parts of attacks, from conducting initial analysis of networks and gaining access to moving within systems and preparing data to be exported.
> “It’s really an all-in-one product,” says Jacob Larsen, an offensive security researcher and founder of security firm Cypen. “Previous iterations of AI agent pen-testing tools would either only do reconnaissance—like the scanning and analysis [of targets]—and some would only do testing. This is really a point-and-shoot weapon.”
> As with other AI hacking frameworks, Artex isn’t an AI product itself. Instead, it is essentially a guide that points external frontier and open-source AI models—that can be connected to it via APIs—to a series of existing penetration testing tools and processes. People using Artex or other similar setups can give simple, natural-language prompts to begin their operations. “Launch a penetration attack on [Redacted victim] to gain access to the site’s admin panel, database, or server,” one set of hackers prompted Artex, according to researchers at the security firm Check Point.
> Once the instructions have been issued, multiple AI agents then carry them out. One agent will break down the plans into a series of tasks, others will try to perform these actions, and the system will then present its findings. Safety guardrails in the underlying AI models, particularly those from frontier labs, can stop hacking activity when they detect it. Increasingly, however, free Chinese and abliterated models are getting better at breaking into systems.
> “It's fast; it’s efficient,” Guillaume Valadon, a researcher at security firm GitGuardian, says of Artex. Valadon and others say the simplicity of the tools makes it easier for unskilled wannabe hackers to try to enter the market—even if they have no clue about what they’re doing. “It lowers the bar,” Valadon says. “I would say my grandmother can do it, except that she doesn't have a laptop, but the bar is that low.”
> As a result, a flurry of reports from cybersecurity companies have linked Artex use to attempted and successful hacks—often by Chinese-speaking cybercriminals trying to make money. These include the theft of personal information from thousands of South Korean financial institutions, potential cryptocurrency theft, and hunting for exposed login details on GitHub.
> “A variety of malicious cyber actors have used Artex to conduct campaigns targeting organizations globally across multiple sectors, including financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, health care, manufacturing, telecommunications, and legal industries,” the FBI warned in an alert about Artex last week.
> In October, China-linked hackers known as Vapor Panda used Artex to target more than 200 organizations, including think tanks, semiconductor and defense firms in the US, and government foreign ministries in Europe and elsewhere, according to security firm CrowdStrike. Microsoft spotted Chinese hackers that it tracks as Storm-0940 using Artex to try to sign in to Microsoft 365 setups following a supply chain attack. It took hackers less than three hours to gain privileged access to systems.
> On October 8, the Autumn-27 developer removed Artex from GitHub, stating in a comment that they are “no way associated with these malicious attacks” and that the tools were developed for “educational and research purposes.” An email WIRED sent to an address linked to the developer did not receive a response.
> Despite the developer pulling Artex, multiple versions of the framework have been copied and continue to be developed and used, alongside other similar tools. Valadon says GitGuardian has documented 45 different AI attack frameworks so far, with CyberstrikeAI, Hexstrike, CAIRN, and PentAGI being frequently mentioned by researchers. They all work in similar ways, with some slightly different technical capabilities. One silver lining for people defending against attacks using such tools is that they’re currently easy to spot.
> “These tools are not stealthy right now,” says Silas Cutler, principal security researcher at internet security firm Censys. Many of the attacks create a lot of noise in systems—making thousands of probes in quick succession. For instance, agentic coding platform Dosu said Artex was used to send 80,000 requests to its systems in just 90 minutes. Researchers say that basic security fundamentals—patching software, not using default credentials or exposing secrets, and monitoring for unusual network activity—can help defend against many of the approaches from those using Artex.
> Pinpointing the number of cybercriminals using Artex and other frameworks isn’t easy; however, thousands of instances of the systems being set up have been exposed to the internet, according to analysis by Censys and the Shadowserver Foundation. Perhaps hinting at the sophistication of those using Artex, researchers have found multiple instances of the tool left unsecured and fully open to the internet, allowing them to inspect how operators are using it.
> Last week, Cutler says, two exposed Artex servers appeared to show Chinese native speakers targeting other Chinese entities. “In one of the cases, it was a university that was being targeted with a password spraying attack, and it has all of that vibe of a student trying to change their grades,” he says.
> “There is a level of this activity that’s occurring that is likely organized, sophisticated, criminal activity,” Cutler says. “There is also, in parallel, likely a subset of the activity that falls more into that juvenile crime realm.”

### Pangram flags 99 percent of an award-winning Peruvian novel as AI-generated, but the publisher stands by its author

- Substantive Intelligence Report:
> AI detection tool Pangram flags 99 percent of the award-winning novel "Donde el agua trabaja"by Peruvian author David Silva Rojas as AI-generated. Despite these allegations, Mexican publisher Almadía is standing by the award after reviewing documents from the author, according to an essay in The Point Magazine. According to the newspaper El País, Pangram had also attributed more than 80 percent of text from interviews, an essay, and the author's Instagram denial to AI.
> In her essay, the author accuses Latin American critics of ignoring Pangram's test results and dismissing the allegations wholesale as racist. She compares the debate to the confirmed use of AI by Thélyson Orélien, as well as accusations involving the Caine Prize and Jamir Nazir, who kept his award. She also argues that literary juries often favor clichéd stories about minorities, which language models can easily imitate. Publisher Gallimard reportedly plans to screen manuscripts with Pangram starting next year.
> In the US, the Authors Guild represents writers' interests. The organization warns against using AI detectors as the sole basis for decisions, even though Pangram reliably identified human-written texts as such in its tests.
